props.text: A contract row proves that 2 sides agree on their messages. The 2 proposers disagree on whether this plan has 2 contract rows: the setup record (VR-062) and the note format (VR-042). Which reading?

**A.** Both are contract rows, and both boundaries count as having contract tests (the Claude proposer). Cost: VR-042 checks a text against its parser, which is closer to a lockstep check than to 2 parts agreeing.

**B.** Neither is a contract row: VR-042 is static, VR-062 is integration, and both boundaries get a proposed ticket (the Codex proposer). Cost: the record readers already have tests that can take the new line; a ticket for that defers 1 small test.

**C.** Split them: VR-062 is a contract row, because setup's real writer writes the record and each real reader reads it; VR-042 is static, and the note boundary gets a ticket to replay recorded notes through the parser (my reconcile).
Each row gets the level that matches what it runs: 2 real programs agree on the record, but the note has only 1 program and a text.
props.label: Recommended: C

items.title: How 2 boundaries count: the install record and the milestone note

props.text: A Codex main agent gets live rows for start, the queue, Ctrl+Enter, the 2 worked examples and the wrap-up. Feedback from the main pane (VR-044) and the setup journey (VR-056, VR-057) run on Claude only. Add Codex rows?
**A.** Add 2 Codex rows: main-pane feedback, and the setup journey that confirms a path. Cost: about 20 more minutes of live run, agent-run.
**B.** Add 1 Codex row for main-pane feedback only. Cost: the setup step on Codex stays unproven live.
**C.** Keep both Claude-only. Cost: a Codex main agent that drops the error text from feedback ships unseen.
Both are main-agent behaviour that each harness reads from text on its own, and an agent runs them at small cost.
props.label: Recommended: A
